Euclid's Segment Division

GeometryConstructionsFractions
Game: See how parallel lines can split a segment into equal pieces without measuring it.
How to play: Drag the dots A, B and C, press + or − to choose how many pieces you want, and tick Show names or Show hint.
3 parts
Look for the math

Draw a sloping line through one end of a segment, step off equal marks on it, then draw parallel lines back. The places where they land on the segment are exactly equally spaced. No ruler needed.

Step off equal marks

Let the segment be BC. Draw a line through B at a positive angle to BC and put A on it. Call the step from B to A d = A − B. Starting at B, the marks are B, B + d (that is A), B + 2d, and so on up to B + Nd, written BN. Every one of those steps has the same length, copied from the first one.

Why the cuts come out equal

Join BN to C and draw through each mark Bi a parallel to that line. It meets the segment at Di. The triangles B Bi Di and B BN C share the angle at B and have parallel third sides, so they are similar triangles with scale i/N:

Di = B + (i/N)(C − B)

That is the page's exact claim: the parallels cross BC at points that divide it into N equal parts. The logic test confirms it for every N the applet allows (1 to 20) and many positions of A, B and C, and compares the crossings with a second transcription of the applet's own line-intersection code. Moving A changes the marks but never the crosses.

What the applet leaves out

The page asks for a positive angle: if A is dragged onto BC, the parallel lines lie along BC and the original applet's intersection divides by zero. This page keeps the marks visible but hides the parallel lines and crossings in that case. The page shows the applet twice, once with Show = 0 and once with Show = 1; the boxes here start as both shown, following the Elements illustration, and can be ticked off.

Try A far away from B and then very close: the crosses on BC stay put. Turn on Show hint to see the matching equal-length marks on both lines.
